“Listen to what I am saying. I have learned despair’s language and know it by heart, for I am Despair itself. What a strange creature I am: joyful, triumphant Despair. Yet those words are wrong, for the wave may be dark without being bitter. We lie down, close our eyes with a gentle good night, and wake to freedom. Come, then, linger no longer! See this pleasant drink! Imagine that a kindly spirit invites you, not a human girl. In a voice meant to persuade you—oh, if only it could!—I say, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I kept my eyes on his face. His extraordinary beauty, the heavenly compassion shining in his eyes, and his gentle but earnest look of protest and wonder changed my intense feelings before he spoke a word. All the hardness of despair left me, and only the tenderest sorrow remained. I saw that his eyes were wet too as he took both my hands. Sitting beside me, he said:

“What you ask me to do is a sad thing, my dearest friend. Your suffering must be deep indeed to fill your mind with such unhappy thoughts. You long to die, yet you fear death and want me beside you. But I am less brave than you, and even with your company I dare not die. Listen, and then consider whether you should persuade me to join you. Consider it even if the overwhelming force of your despair could make dark death so inviting that beautiful heaven seemed gloomy beside it. Please hear someone who has also fed desperate thoughts and impatiently wished for death, but who has finally stamped that phantom beneath his feet and destroyed its sting. You have played Despair with me; now let me play Una and lead you safely out of his dark cave. Listen, and allow yourself to be moved by words that contain no selfish feeling.

“We do not understand this vast world, with its strange mixture of good and evil. Yet we have been placed here and told to live and hope. I do not know what we should hope for, but there is some good beyond our reach that we must seek. That is our work on earth. If misfortune attacks, we must struggle against it, push it aside, and keep searching for what our nature makes us desire. I do not know whether this promise of future good prepares us for another life. Perhaps it means only that we, as workers in God’s vineyard, must help make the path easier for those who come after us.

“I cannot say how long I remained like this. It must have been quite some time, though, because when I partly regained consciousness, dawn was breaking. The balloon floated at an enormous height above an empty ocean, and there was no land anywhere along the vast horizon. Yet waking brought far less agony than might have been expected. In fact, my calm examination of my position showed clear signs that I was beginning to lose my mind. I lifted each hand to my eyes in turn, wondering what could have swollen the veins and turned the fingernails so horribly black. Next I examined my head with great care, shaking it repeatedly and feeling it all over, until I convinced myself it was not bigger than my balloon, as I had rather strongly suspected. Then, with an air of understanding, I searched both pockets of my trousers. Finding my writing tablets and toothpick case missing, I tried to explain their disappearance. When I could not, I felt more upset than I can express. I now noticed severe discomfort in my left ankle joint, and a faint awareness of my situation began to dawn on me. Strangely enough, I felt neither surprise nor horror. If I felt anything, it was a sort of amused satisfaction at the cleverness I was about to show in getting myself out of trouble. Not for an instant did I doubt that I would eventually be safe. I spent several minutes in deep thought. I distinctly remember pressing my lips together again and again, laying my forefinger beside my nose, and making the other gestures and faces common to men comfortably seated in armchairs, considering a difficult or important problem. Once I thought I had properly organized my ideas, I carefully and slowly reached behind my back and undid the large iron buckle on my trouser waistband. The buckle had three prongs. These were somewhat rusty and very difficult to turn on their pivot. With some effort, however, I raised them until they stood at right angles to the buckle’s frame. I was pleased to find that they stayed firmly in that position. Holding this newly made tool between my teeth, I began to undo the knot of my neckcloth. I had to stop several times to rest before I could manage it, but eventually I succeeded.

“On that subject, then, I will always remain silent. You can be certain that once we are married, no unkind reproach will ever escape my lips.”

At this point she absolutely had to interrupt him.

“You are getting ahead of yourself, sir,” she exclaimed. “You forget that I have not answered. Let me do so without any further delay. Thank you for the compliment you are paying me. I fully appreciate the honor of your proposal, but I have no choice except to decline it.”

“I am well aware,” replied Mr. Collins, waving his hand formally, “that young ladies commonly refuse a man they secretly intend to accept when he first asks for their affection. Sometimes they repeat that refusal a second or even a third time. Your words therefore do not discourage me at all, and I hope we will be married before long.”

“Really, sir,” Elizabeth cried, “that is a remarkable hope after what I have said. I assure you that I am not one of those young women—if any such women exist—who would dare gamble their happiness on being asked again. My refusal is entirely serious. You could not make me happy, and I am convinced that no woman in the world would be less likely to make you happy than I would. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine knew me, I am sure she would consider me unsuitable for the position in every respect.”

“If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins with great seriousness—“but I cannot imagine that her Ladyship would disapprove of you at all. And you may be sure that when I next have the honor of seeing her, I will speak most highly of your modesty, thrift, and other admirable qualities.”

“Truly, Mr. Collins, there is no need to praise me. You must allow me to decide for myself and do me the courtesy of believing what I say. I wish you every happiness and prosperity, and by refusing to marry you, I am doing everything I can to protect you from the opposite. By proposing, you must have satisfied your sense of consideration toward my family. Whenever you inherit the Longbourn estate, you can take possession without blaming yourself. We may therefore regard this matter as finally settled.” She stood as she spoke and would have left the room if Mr. Collins had not addressed her again.

“When I next have the honor of speaking to you about this, I hope your answer will be more favorable than the one you have given today. Still, I am far from accusing you of cruelty now. I know that women traditionally reject a man’s first proposal, and perhaps you have already said as much to encourage me as a truly modest woman could properly allow herself to say.”
